Hemolytic Anemia

drug-induced immune hemolysis and hereditary spherocytosis · latency, the Coombs test and the smear name the mechanism, then map it to its assayWhich drug and how long ago, is the direct Coombs test positive, and are the platelets and liver enzymes normal?

DiagnosisPracticeManagement
Bottom line

Confirm hemolysis, then name the mechanism. Anemia with an unconjugated bilirubin, dark urine and normal liver enzymes is hemolysis; the enzymes, not the pain, separate it from obstruction.

  • Hapten drug hemolysis: a stable hapten such as high-dose penicillin or a cephalosporin such as cefotetan binds the red-cell surface, IgG (immunoglobulin G) attaches to the drug-cell complex, and splenic macrophages destroy the cell: extravascular, with spherocytes, typically after 7 to 10 days of high-dose penicillin.
  • Immune-complex drug hemolysis: the drug, mainly ceftriaxone or piperacillin, forms complexes with drug-specific antibodies that fix complement for intravascular destruction; the Coombs test is usually positive for complement, not IgG; after earlier exposure it can follow a single dose within hours.
  • Hereditary spherocytosis: Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia with jaundice and splenomegaly; mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC) above 36%, because membrane loss dehydrates the cell, the one common anemia with a high MCHC; splenectomy needs pneumococcal, meningococcal and Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) vaccination first.
  • Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia: IgG against red cells; a positive Coombs test is the only line separating it from hereditary spherocytosis.
  • Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency: oxidant hemolysis 1 to 3 days (24 to 72 hours) after the trigger, with bite cells, Heinz bodies and a negative Coombs test.
  • Cold agglutinin hemolysis: IgM (immunoglobulin M) fixes complement, so the test shows C3 (complement component 3) only.

Spherocytes mean a membrane defect (hereditary spherocytosis) or an IgG antibody (warm autoimmune or hapten drug hemolysis), plus ABO (blood group) incompatibility in a newborn. The Coombs test separates membrane (negative) from antibody (positive); the history (a drug, lupus, the first day of life) separates the antibodies. A normal platelet count excludes the consumptive causes.

Diagnosis
Hemolysis in a child: the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe tell
Drug-induced immune hemolysisHigh-dose penicillin or a cephalosporin such as cefotetan: stable hapten, IgG, extravascular; ceftriaxone or piperacillin: immune complexes fix complement, intravascular; also a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) such as diclofenacHapten: typically after 7 to 10 days of high-dose penicillin, Coombs IgG. Immune complex: can follow a single dose within hours after earlier exposure, Coombs C3. Drug hemolysis may take hours or several months. Platelets usually normal

G6PD deficiencyX-linked, so mostly boys; normal between episodes; oxidant stress depletes glutathione: infection, sulfonamides, dapsone, nitrofurantoin, primaquine or fava beans; African, Mediterranean, Middle Eastern or Asian ancestry1 to 3 days (24 to 72 hours) after the trigger; sudden dark urine with back or abdominal pain; bite cells, Heinz bodies on crystal violet stain, Coombs negative, MCHC normal

Practice
  1. 5-year-old girl treated for pneumonia has dark urine and abdominal pain Received ceftriaxone for otitis media last year Began one hour after today's intravenous ceftriaxone dose mild upper abdominal tenderness hemoglobin 6.3 g/dL · platelets 285,000/mm³ · liver enzymes normal → Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test → hemolysis within an hour of a ceftriaxone dose, in a child sensitized by the earlier course, is immune: ceftriaxone mainly forms drug-antibody immune complexes that fix complement, so the direct antiglobulin test is positive for C3, with or without IgG. Oxidative hemolysis begins 24 to 72 hours after exposure, and ceftriaxone is not a typical oxidant. A normal platelet count excludes disseminated intravascular coagulation, so a fibrinogen level adds nothing
  2. 7-year-old boy has had intermittent jaundice for months His father has the same anemia spleen palpable 3 cm below the costal margin spherocytes on the smear hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL · MCHC 38% · direct Coombs negative → Eosin-5-maleimide binding test → spherocytes with a negative Coombs test mean a membrane defect; the MCHC above 36% and the affected father support it but do not decide it. Eosin-5-maleimide binding by flow cytometry shows reduced fluorescence; osmotic fragility is the older equivalent. CD55 and CD59 testing is for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, and hemoglobinopathies give target cells or sickled forms, never spherocytes
  3. 7-year-old boy has dark urine on day 3 of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole bite cells on the smear Heinz bodies on a crystal violet stain Direct antiglobulin test negative HR 118/min · hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL · platelets 240,000/mm³ → Stop the drug and measure glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase after recovery → bite cells and Heinz bodies with a negative direct antiglobulin test 1 to 3 days (24 to 72 hours) after an oxidant are oxidative, not immune, hemolysis. Stop the drug; measured during the episode, the surviving young cells carry near-normal enzyme and read falsely normal, so the level waits until weeks after recovery
  4. 24-year-old woman has 2 weeks of fatigue and jaundice Systemic lupus erythematosus diagnosed 3 years ago spherocytes on the smear direct Coombs test positive for IgG HR 104/min · hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL · platelets 220,000/mm³ → Prednisone → spherocytes with a positive direct Coombs test in lupus are warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia: IgG against red cells, subacute. The Coombs test is the only line separating it from hereditary spherocytosis, so eosin-5-maleimide binding, which confirms a membrane defect, is not needed; splenectomy is not the first step
  5. 4-year-old girl hospitalized with sepsis has oozing from line sites and dark urine Receiving intravenous antibiotics schistocytes on the smear BP 82/48 mm Hg · hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL · platelets 18,000/mm³ · fibrinogen 80 mg/dL → Treat the underlying sepsis with coagulation support → schistocytes, severe thrombocytopenia and a low fibrinogen in sepsis are a consumptive coagulopathy: treat the cause. Drug-induced immune hemolysis does not usually explain schistocytes with a low fibrinogen, so stopping the antibiotic answers the wrong process, and the direct antiglobulin test looks for an antibody when schistocytes with a low platelet count mean a clot
  6. 7-year-old boy has intermittent jaundice and an enlarged spleen No family history of anemia, jaundice or gallstones spherocytes on the smear hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL · MCHC 37% · direct Coombs test negative → Hereditary spherocytosis → spherocytes with a negative Coombs test and an MCHC above 36% are a membrane defect even without an affected parent: a meaningful fraction are de novo or recessive. Warm autoimmune hemolysis is Coombs positive, and paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria brings cytopenias and a bland smear in an adult
  7. 5-year-old girl has dark urine and pallor on day 2 of intravenous ceftriaxone for pneumonia Had a ceftriaxone course last year hemoglobinuria on urinalysis Direct antiglobulin test positive for C3 and IgG HR 112/min · hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL · platelets 250,000/mm³ → Discontinue the ceftriaxone → hemoglobinuria suggests the immune-complex mechanism, and stopping the drug is the treatment and usually resolves the hemolysis within hours to days. Glucocorticoids and intravenous immunoglobulin are reserved for severe cases and never justify continuing the drug; plasma exchange has been reported as a rescue in life-threatening cases, not a first step in a stable child. Ceftriaxone hemolysis is C3-positive, often with IgG, and is more common after an earlier course
  8. 30-year-old man has dark urine on waking most mornings new hepatic vein thrombosis on ultrasound Direct Coombs test negative; smear bland Afebrile · hemoglobin 8.8 g/dL · white cells 2,900/mm³ · platelets 88,000/mm³ → Flow cytometry for CD55 and CD59 → Coombs-negative hemolysis with cytopenias, thrombosis at an odd site and a bland smear: an acquired clone whose red cells lack CD55 and CD59 and undergo complement-mediated intravascular lysis. Eosin-5-maleimide binding confirms a spherocytic membrane defect, and a marrow biopsy further characterizes the disease in the setting of another marrow abnormality; flow cytometry is the gold standard
  9. 15-year-old girl has jaundice and fatigue 10 days into an atypical pneumonia No new medications direct antiglobulin test positive for C3, negative for IgG cold agglutinins present Afebrile · hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL · platelets 230,000/mm³ → Mycoplasma-associated cold agglutinin hemolysis → atypical pneumonia drives IgM against the I antigen, which fixes complement, so the direct antiglobulin test shows C3 only; the hemolysis follows the infection, whose cold agglutinins can turn positive after 7 to 10 days. Drug-induced immune hemolysis needs a drug, although its immune-complex type also shows complement without IgG, and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency gives bite cells with a negative test
  10. 10-year-old girl has a week of increasing pallor and fatigue Hereditary spherocytosis was diagnosed at age 2 slapped-cheek rashes among classmates at school hemoglobin 5 g/dL, 12 g/dL a week ago · reticulocytes 0.1% → Transfusion → a falling hemoglobin with a low reticulocyte count in a chronic hemolytic patient is parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis until proven otherwise, and transfusion treats an aplastic or hemolytic crisis. Folic acid is for chronic reticulocytosis, and splenectomy is indicated for symptomatic hemolysis or complications such as biliary colic or a persistent aplastic crisis
  11. 8-year-old boy needs an antibiotic for pneumonia Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency was diagnosed at age 3 after an episode of dark urine cough; right lower lobe crackles T 38.6 °C · HR 110/min · oxygen saturation 95% → Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole → oxidant stress depletes glutathione and precipitates hemolysis: sulfonamides do it, as do dapsone, nitrofurantoin, primaquine and fava beans. Neither ceftriaxone nor azithromycin is a typical oxidant
  12. 14-year-old boy has colicky right upper quadrant pain after meals Coombs-negative spherocytic anemia since infancy; father affected mild scleral icterus; spleen tip palpable Afebrile · HR 88/min · hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL · transaminases normal → Right upper quadrant ultrasound → extravascular splenic hemolysis raises the indirect bilirubin and forms pigment stones, so colic after meals earns an ultrasound, the imaging test of choice for gallbladder stones, with cholecystectomy if stones are present. Plain radiographs miss most gallstones, and hepatitis serologies answer a hepatitis that normal transaminases make unlikely
  13. 9-year-old boy develops fever, back pain and dark urine 15 minutes into a packed red cell transfusion after surgery flushed and anxious; no wheeze or rash T 39.0 °C · HR 132/min · BP 92/54 mm Hg → Stop the transfusion immediately → fever, back pain and dark urine minutes into a transfusion are an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction: ABO incompatibility drives complement-mediated intravascular lysis, so the transfusion stops at once. Slowing it with an antipyretic, or an antihistamine and continuing, keeps the incompatible blood running
  14. 10-year-old Black boy has back pain and dark urine since waking First episode; cough and fever 2 days ago, treated with ibuprofen scleral icterus; mild abdominal tenderness Afebrile · HR 104/min · hemoglobin 8.0 g/dL bite cells; crystal violet stain shows inclusions → G6PD deficiency → bite cells, with Heinz bodies as the inclusions on a crystal violet stain, after an infection: activated leukocytes release oxidants that denature hemoglobin, and the episode brings sudden dark urine with back or abdominal pain. Infection is the leading cause of acute hemolysis in this deficiency, so the ibuprofen is not needed to explain it. Sickle cell disease shows sickled forms on the smear, and acute intermittent porphyria darkens the urine without anemia or bite cells
  15. 5-year-old girl with pneumonia has dark urine since this morning after intravenous ceftriaxone Direct antiglobulin test positive for C3 lethargic and pale; dark urine continuing HR 168/min · hemoglobin 4.5 g/dL · platelets 260,000/mm³ → Transfuse and discontinue the offending drug → severity gates transfusion: stop the drug and transfuse when the anemia is severe. Glucocorticoids are for severe cases but do not replace the transfusion, and observation alone leaves a hemoglobin of 4.5 with tachycardia and lethargy untreated
  16. 8-year-old boy has fever and looks ill Hereditary spherocytosis was diagnosed at age 2; splenectomy a year ago ill-appearing; no focal source found T 39.5 °C · HR 150/min · BP 90/56 mm Hg → Blood cultures and intravenous ceftriaxone now → treat every fever after splenectomy as sepsis until proven otherwise: blood cultures and intravenous antibiotics now, not oral antibiotics or observation
  17. 7-year-old boy has pallor and dark urine on day 9 of high-dose intravenous penicillin Direct antiglobulin test positive for IgG spherocytes on the smear; liver enzymes normal hemoglobin 7.6 g/dL · platelets 270,000/mm³ → The drug binds the erythrocyte surface as a hapten, IgG attaches, and splenic macrophages destroy the cell → high-dose penicillin is a stable hapten, and its hemolysis typically follows 7 to 10 days of the drug: it binds the red-cell membrane, IgG attaches to the drug-cell complex and splenic macrophages clear it, an extravascular hemolysis with spherocytes and a direct antiglobulin test positive for IgG. Heinz bodies come from oxidant injury with a negative test, and complement-fixing IgM gives a C3-only result
  18. 18-hour-old boy born at term has visible jaundice Mother blood group O positive; infant A positive spherocytes on the smear direct antiglobulin test weakly positive Total serum bilirubin above the phototherapy threshold, below the exchange level HR 142/min → Phototherapy → jaundice on the first day with a group O mother, a group A infant, spherocytes and a weakly positive direct antiglobulin test is ABO hemolytic disease of the newborn, the antibody cause of spherocytes on the first day of life; phototherapy treats a bilirubin above the phototherapy threshold. Eosin-5-maleimide binding looks for hereditary spherocytosis, and the bilirubin is below the exchange level, so exchange transfusion is not indicated
  19. 8-year-old boy has pallor, jaundice and dark urine on day 2 of a febrile pneumonia G6PD deficiency was diagnosed at age 1; no antibiotic given bite cells on the smear; direct antiglobulin test negative T 38.9 °C · hemoglobin 7.9 g/dL → Oxidants from activated leukocytes denature hemoglobin → infection alone is an oxidant stress: activated leukocytes release oxidants, and red cells short of NADPH (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate) cannot regenerate glutathione. Cold-reacting IgM gives a C3-positive test, and red cells lacking CD55 and CD59 belong to paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, with cytopenias
  20. 6-year-old boy is reviewed 2 days after his piperacillin was stopped Treated for hemolysis with a positive direct antiglobulin test mild residual jaundice; energy improving hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL, up from 7.9 g/dL · HR 96/min → Observation without glucocorticoids → drug withdrawal is the treatment and usually resolves the hemolysis within hours to days; a stable, rising hemoglobin shows it working. Glucocorticoids and intravenous immunoglobulin are reserved for severe cases
  21. 5-year-old boy from a Greek family has pallor, jaundice and dark urine since this morning Ate fava beans 2 days ago Direct antiglobulin test negative hemoglobin 7.9 g/dL · reticulocytes raised · HR 118/min → Bite cells → oxidized hemoglobin precipitates as Heinz bodies, and splenic macrophages bite them out; the Heinz bodies themselves need a supravital stain such as crystal violet. Spherocytes mean a membrane defect or a warm antibody, and schistocytes mean cells sheared in damaged small vessels
  22. 16-year-old girl has fatigue that limits her sport Hereditary spherocytosis was diagnosed at age 4; splenectomy is planned gallstones on ultrasound; cholecystectomy planned alongside hemoglobin 8 g/dL · reticulocytes 12% · HR 96/min → Pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib vaccination before surgery → Hib vaccination joins the pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccines before splenectomy for moderate to severe disease, deferred, ideally, until after age 6, so neither an influenza vaccine alone nor no vaccination is enough
  23. 5-year-old boy has dark urine 3 days after starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole bite cells on the smear; Heinz bodies on supravital stain He is still actively hemolyzing today HR 124/min · hemoglobin 7.4 g/dL · reticulocytes 9% → Measuring G6PD activity during the acute episode → during acute hemolysis the surviving young cells carry near-normal enzyme and read falsely normal, so the assay waits weeks. Stopping the drug and supportive care are right now
Management
Treatment by mechanism Drug-induced immune hemolysis – stop the drug, which usually resolves the hemolysis within hours to days (penicillin hapten hemolysis typically ceases a few days to 2 weeks after stopping); transfuse if the anemia is severe; glucocorticoids, of questionable benefit, and intravenous immunoglobulin only for severe cases, and never while continuing the drug · Hereditary spherocytosis – folic acid for chronic reticulocytosis; transfusion for an aplastic or hemolytic crisis · Splenectomy – for moderate to severe disease, deferred, ideally, until after age 6, preceded by pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib vaccination; cholecystectomy too if pigment stones are present · After splenectomy – the hemolysis stops but the defect does not: spherocytes persist and Howell-Jolly bodies appear; treat every fever as sepsis until proven otherwise
Aplastic crisis A falling hemoglobin with a low reticulocyte count in any chronic hemolytic patient is parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis until proven otherwise.
Smear clues in hemolysis
Smear findingWhat made itPoints to
Sickle cellsCrescent cells from polymerized hemoglobin SSickle cell disease; a crisis brings severe pain
Target cellsToo much membrane for the hemoglobin insideThalassemia, microcytic and chronic rather than acute; also hemoglobin C and liver disease
SpherocytesMembrane lost, leaving small round cells without central pallorHereditary spherocytosis, warm autoimmune or hapten drug hemolysis; ABO disease in a newborn
Bite cells and Heinz bodiesOxidized hemoglobin precipitates as Heinz bodies, and splenic macrophages bite them outG6PD deficiency after an oxidant trigger
SchistocytesRed cells sheared in damaged small vessels or on a mechanical valveMicroangiopathic hemolysis: HUS, TTP, DIC
Latency is a diagnostic variable Immune-complex drug hemolysis can arrive within hours of a dose in a patient sensitized by earlier exposure; hapten hemolysis typically builds over 7 to 10 days of high-dose penicillin; oxidative hemolysis comes in 1 to 3 days (24 to 72 hours); cold agglutinin hemolysis follows the pneumonia that caused it, whose cold agglutinins can turn positive after 7 to 10 days. Symptoms one hour after a dose are too fast for oxidative injury. Hemolysis within hours of a ceftriaxone or piperacillin dose is immune-complex, and the direct antiglobulin test reveals it, positive for C3; IgG without C3 usually marks the hapten type.
Reading the labs and the pain The MCHC is the only red-cell index that rises in a common anemia, and the red cell distribution width (RDW) rises with it. A normal MCV does not exclude hemolysis, because a 10% reticulocytosis inflates it. Hereditary spherocytosis hemolyzes extravascularly, with indirect bilirubin, splenomegaly and pigment stones; PNH and severe G6PD deficiency hemolyze intravascularly, with hemoglobinuria, low haptoglobin and high LDH. Dark urine is hemoglobinuria or urobilinogen; with normal liver tests it is red cells, not bile. Severe hemolysis causes abdominal or back pain from red-cell destruction in the vertebral bodies, liver and spleen, while biliary obstruction would hurt considerably more. A normal creatinine argues against a microangiopathy and against massive intravascular hemolysis.
Common wrong answers A G6PD level during the episode, or for hemolysis one hour after a drug that is not a typical oxidant. Abdominal computed tomography or liver ultrasound: obstruction brings severe pain with raised alkaline phosphatase and transaminases, and imaging cannot explain a hemoglobin of 6.3. Serum fibrinogen: DIC needs severe thrombocytopenia with prolonged clotting times. Retroperitoneal hemorrhage: back pain with acute anemia, but it follows trauma or a coagulopathy; a normal prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time with a normal platelet count and no injury exclude it. Anaphylaxis to a beta-lactam: seconds to minutes, with rash and edema, and no anemia. CD55 and CD59 testing just because the hemolysis is Coombs negative: PNH means cytopenias, a bland smear and acquired disease, not spherocytes in a boy whose father is affected. G6PD deficiency for a boy with jaundice: it needs an oxidant trigger and is not passed father to son. Hemoglobinopathy: the right class of inherited red-cell disorder, but it gives targets or sickles, never spherocytes.
Decoy note In the first item, upper abdominal tenderness and dark urine tempt a biliary reading when symptoms are read before the laboratory values. Mycoplasma cold agglutinins also give a C3-positive direct antiglobulin test, so the test is still the right one, and the one-hour latency after a ceftriaxone dose points to the drug.
Pairs with Part I Anemia with Thrombocytopenia: hemolysis with thrombocytopenia, where the smear and the coagulation studies identify a different process; an isolated hemolytic anemia is one process, a hemolytic anemia with thrombocytopenia another. Part I Respiratory Infection in a Child carries the Mycoplasma cold agglutinin association. Related conditions without their own brief: warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (ask: is the direct Coombs test positive?) shares jaundice, anemia and spherocytes with hereditary spherocytosis, and paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (ask: are the white cells and platelets normal?).
Transferable rule

When two mechanisms or diagnoses share a syndrome or a smear finding, the case supplies the attribute that separates them, usually an exposure and an interval or one test; choose the test for the mechanism, not the finding they share, then map the disease to its confirmatory assay. Spherocytes with a normal platelet count mean an antibody or a membrane; schistocytes with a low platelet count mean a clot.

Antibody Deficiencies

infection pattern · B-cell count first · isotype panel · class-switch failure · what each defect predictsAre B cells present, and which isotype is preserved or elevated?

Source vignette Pt — toddler with intensive care unit (ICU)-level pneumococcal pneumonia, tympanic membrane perforation with otorrhea, weight below the 3rd percentile · Labs — IgM 450, IgG 250, IgA 24; neutropenia (15% of 9,000) · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned CD40 ligand deficiency, X-linked agammaglobulinemia, common variable immunodeficiency, selective IgA deficiency, hyper-IgE syndrome, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)
The decision point

ICU-level pneumococcal pneumonia, tympanic perforation with otorrhea, and weight below the 3rd percentile establish a primary immunodeficiency rather than ordinary toddler illness. The infection history does not show which one. The panel shows IgM 450 against IgG 250 and IgA 24. XLA (X-linked agammaglobulinemia) requires IgM to be low, and CVID (common variable immunodeficiency) requires it to be low or normal. Selective IgA deficiency and Job syndrome require a normal IgM. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome and HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) require a non-immunologic finding this child does not have: microthrombocytopenia and an inverted CD4/CD8, respectively. An isolated elevation of IgM with everything downstream absent is class-switch failure. CD40 ligand on the T cell cannot engage CD40 on the B cell, so the B cell stays locked on its native isotype. The neutropenia (15% of 9,000) is a confirmatory detail: it accompanies CD40 ligand deficiency and does not belong to XLA or CVID.

Defining criteria Class switching (isotype switch recombination) — the CD40L(T cell)–CD40(B cell) interaction that lets an IgM-committed B cell rearrange to IgG, IgA, or IgE; when it fails, IgM is preserved or elevated and every other isotype falls · The CD40L signature — B cells normal, IgM ↑, IgG ↓, IgA ↓, IgE ↓. B and T cell counts are normal; they are dysfunctional, not absent · The B-cell count is the first gate — low or absent CD19+ B cells → X-linked agammaglobulinemia; normal B cells → the block is downstream of B-cell development, and the isotype pattern names it
Pertinent positives & negatives IgM 450 with IgG 250 and IgA 24 — class-switch failure; simultaneously excludes XLA (all isotypes low) and CVID (IgM low or normal, never elevated) and selective IgA deficiency (requires normal IgG and IgM) · Neutropenia (absolute neutrophil count, ANC ≈1,350) — common in CD40L deficiency; not a feature of XLA or CVID · Lymphocytes 75%, CD4/CD8 2.2 — normal lymphocyte compartment; excludes HIV, where leukopenia and an inverted ratio are expected · Platelets 260,000 — excludes Wiskott-Aldrich, which requires small, low platelets · Age 14 months with disease since early infancy — argues against CVID, which surfaces in adolescents and young adults · Vaccinations up to date, yet invasive pneumococcal disease — vaccine failure from absent opsonizing IgG, not from missed doses · Lymphadenopathy — separates HIV from SCID (severe combined immunodeficiency): HIV causes generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly from chronic immune activation, while SCID has absent or tiny lymph nodes because there are no lymphocytes to populate them

SCID: the newborn screen and the cure Defect — gene defects stop T-cell development; B cells fail without T-cell help, so antibody is low too; X-linked or autosomal recessive · Presentation — in the first months: severe viral, fungal (thrush) and opportunistic (Pneumocystis) infection, chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive · Labs and exam — lymphopenia with low CD4 and CD8 counts, hypogammaglobulinemia, no palpable nodes or tonsils · Newborn screen — part of US newborn screening: absent T-cell receptor excision circles (TRECs) on the dried blood spot; lymphocyte flow cytometry confirms · Treatment — hematopoietic stem cell transplant as early as possible; no live vaccines · Not SCID — Bruton agammaglobulinemia has absent B cells but normal T cells and bacterial rather than fungal or opportunistic infection; CVID starts later with normal T- and B-cell counts; CGD has normal lymphocytes and immunoglobulins
Syndromic immunodeficiencies: the tell off the panel Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome — WATER: Wiskott-Aldrich, Thrombocytopenia with small platelets, Eczema, Recurrent infections; X-linked; bleeding at circumcision or from the umbilical stump in early infancy; T-cell dysfunction and low immunoglobulins worsen with age; stem cell transplant · Hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome — FATED: coarse Facies (broad nose, prominent forehead), cold staphylococcal Abscesses, retained primary Teeth, high IgE with eosinophilia, Dermatologic eczema; autosomal dominant; impaired Th17 signaling; skin care and antibiotic prophylaxis · Ataxia-telangiectasia — autosomal recessive defect in DNA break repair; early childhood progressive cerebellar ataxia and poorly coordinated eye and head movements, then telangiectasias of the conjunctivae and face; recurrent sinopulmonary infection; high malignancy risk; genetic testing confirms · Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis with polyendocrinopathy — AIRE deficiency breaks thymic negative selection, giving a T-cell defect against Candida plus autoimmunity; chronic Candida of skin, mouth and nails with hypoparathyroidism (hypocalcemia, seizure), adrenal insufficiency, type 1 diabetes and thyroiditis
Management, in one line Management is to replace what is missing and cover what the defect exposes. Give immunoglobulin replacement in XLA, CVID and CD40 ligand deficiency; in CD40 ligand deficiency, add TMP-SMX (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) prophylaxis against Pneumocystis. In severe antibody deficiency, avoid live vaccines such as MMR (measles, mumps and rubella); in T-cell defects, avoid all live vaccines. In selective IgA deficiency, IVIG (intravenous immunoglobulin) does not help, and transfusions use washed or IgA-deficient products. Allogeneic HSCT (hematopoietic stem cell transplantation) is the curative therapy for CD40 ligand deficiency.
Long-term treatment: match it to the defect CVID and XLA — lifelong IVIG: the B cells cannot make antibody, so it is supplied; infections fall, but the autoimmune and malignancy risk of CVID remains · SCID — hematopoietic stem cell transplant, as early as possible · Complete DiGeorge syndrome (no thymus) — cultured thymus tissue transplant · CGD — interferon gamma, the immunomodulator, plus TMP-SMX and itraconazole prophylaxis · Cellular (T-cell) defects — antiviral and antifungal prophylaxis · CVID, an antibody defect with normal T cells — needs antibody replacement, not a transplant or an immunomodulator, although each is right for some other defect
Decision spine Is this beyond normal childhood illness? — ICU pneumonia, perforated tympanic membranes, weight <3rd percentile → yes, work it up as primary immunodeficiency · Are B cells / lymphocytes present? — Normal → not XLA (X-linked agammaglobulinemia) · Is IgM high, normal, or low? — High with everything else low → class-switch failure → CD40L deficiency · Is any isotype normal or high? — IgG normal with IgA alone low → selective IgA deficiency; IgE very high → Job · Is every isotype high? — IgG, IgA and IgM all high is polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. The primary antibody deficiencies all lower IgG or IgA. With thrush, adenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly, test for HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) · Any finding off the panel? — Small low platelets → Wiskott-Aldrich; inverted CD4/CD8 → HIV · Now use the pattern: — which organisms and which treatment does this specific block predict?

Decoy note Lymphocytes at 75% look alarming but are expected. Lymphocytosis accompanies active infection. It also confirms that lymphocyte numbers are intact, which excludes XLA (X-linked agammaglobulinemia). The three bronchiolitis episodes read as ordinary infant viral illness but support CD40 ligand deficiency, which impairs viral defense as well as opsonization. Up-to-date vaccination converts the pneumococcal ICU admission into vaccine failure, an immunodeficiency finding rather than a gap in care.
Pearls High IgM with low IgG/IgA is class-switch failure. Absent B cells is XLA (X-linked agammaglobulinemia). Low IgG with low IgA and/or IgM and B cells present is CVID (common variable immunodeficiency). · Read the panel in a fixed order: B cells, then IgM, then IgG/IgA/IgE. · The missing isotype predicts the organism. No opsonizing IgG → encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, H. influenzae). A broken CD40 ligand–CD40 axis also breaks T-cell licensing of macrophages → Pneumocystis and Cryptosporidium. · Neutropenia alongside hypogammaglobulinemia points at CD40L deficiency rather than XLA. · Selective IgA deficiency is the defect whose management is what you withhold: no IVIG, and washed or IgA-deficient blood products for transfusion. · A severe antibody deficiency contraindicates live vaccines such as MMR, and a defective T-cell limb contraindicates all of them; and replacement IgG likely interferes with later vaccine-titer testing. · A mildly low IgG at 6–9 months in a thriving infant with normal IgM, normal B cells, and protective vaccine titers is transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy: recheck levels, and treatment is conservative. · How NBME framed it: the lead-in asks for a mechanism but lists diseases, and the mother's thrush, chronic diarrhea and weight loss hold the deciding clue.
The physiologic IgG nadir The nadir — maternally derived IgG wanes after birth and troughs at 3 to 6 months, when the infant's own synthesis takes over · Transient hypogammaglobulinemia — that synthesis is delayed and the nadir is prolonged beyond 6 months, with recurrent respiratory infection and atopy · Vaccine response is the most discriminating line on the panel — a normal response excludes common variable immunodeficiency and X-linked agammaglobulinemia at once, whatever the isotype levels say
Pairs with Part I Recurrent Respiratory Infection and Structural Lung Disease shares the complaint of recurrent otitis media and pneumonia in a child. Ask: does the immunoglobulin panel explain it, or does the anatomy? When the panel is normal, that brief covers the structural and mucociliary axis; when an isotype is out of step, this one does. Part I Neutrophil Disorders: Number and Function covers the phagocyte defects: chronic granulomatous disease, leukocyte adhesion deficiency and Chédiak-Higashi. Ask: are the immunoglobulins normal, and is there pus? Part I 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome covers the thymic T-cell defect with hypocalcemia (CATCH-22); ask: is there a conotruncal heart lesion? Part II Infectious Diarrhea follows a patient with common variable immunodeficiency on immunoglobulin replacement who develops Salmonella gastroenteritis. Ask: does the organism point to the immune defect, or to the food it came from?
Transferable rule With recurrent sinopulmonary infection and an immunoglobulin panel, read the pattern rather than recall a disease. Count the B cells, then ask which isotype is preserved. The preserved isotype names the block, and the missing isotypes name the organisms you must cover.
Unchecked attributeWiskott-Aldrich syndrome: eczema plus recurrent infection fits its pattern, but it requires small, low platelets. A normal count excludes it, and atopy is itself a feature of transient hypogammaglobulinemia.
Class-vs-memberBruton agammaglobulinemia: That member of the class requires absent B cells and low IgM; IgM is 450 and the lymphocyte compartment is intact
True-fact-wrong-slotCommon variable immunodeficiency: CVID leaves IgM low or normal but never high, and presents in adolescence or later, not at 14 months
Salient decoyHIV infection: HIV would show leukopenia and a low CD4/CD8 ratio; here the ratio is 2.2 and WBC 9,000. HIV raises IgG in a polyclonal rise, while this panel has IgG 250.
True-fact-wrong-slotIgA deficiency: Isolated IgA deficiency requires normal IgG and IgM; IgG 250 makes the deficiency global-with-a-block, not selective
Class-vs-memberWiskott-Aldrich syndrome: The syndromic member is defined by microthrombocytopenia; platelets are 260,000 and normal-sized, and there is no eczema
Class-vs-memberSevere combined immunodeficiency: It presents in early infancy with lymphopenia, low immunoglobulins and no palpable nodes. A 2-year-old with every isotype high and 2-cm axillary nodes does not fit.
Unchecked attributeWiskott-Aldrich syndrome: Platelets of 95,000 are the lure. It classically has eczema and small platelets, and it is X-linked, while this patient with every isotype high is a girl.
True-fact-wrong-slotCommon variable immunodeficiency: It lowers IgG along with IgA and/or IgM, and it usually starts after puberty. Here every isotype is high at age 2.
True-fact-wrong-slotChronic granulomatous disease: It causes catalase-positive abscesses and granulomas with an abnormal DHR (dihydrorhodamine) test. Immunoglobulins are normal or high in it, so this panel does not exclude it; the thrush, the adenopathy and the mother's illness point to HIV.
Unchecked attributeChédiak-Higashi syndrome: It needs oculocutaneous albinism and neuropathy, and neither is described in the girl with every isotype high.
True-fact-wrong-slotTerminal complement deficiency: It causes recurrent Neisseria infection, not pneumococcal disease with thrush and every isotype high.
Salient decoyCystic fibrosis: Recurrent pneumonia and low weight fit. It causes lung and pancreatic disease, without thrush, adenopathy or a mother with an AIDS-suggestive illness.

Jaundice in a Newborn

timing, direct fraction and Coombs · the sick neonate with a positive screenIs the infant well, and is any of it direct?

WorkupCausesSick neonatePractice
Bottom line

Physiologic jaundice is a conjugation lag: fetal hemoglobin breaks down quickly while hepatic uridine diphosphate (UDP) glucuronosyltransferase is still immature, so unconjugated bilirubin accumulates. A raised direct fraction makes newborn jaundice urgent.

  • Physiologic jaundice: begins after 24 hours, peaks around day 3 to 5, predominantly indirect, resolving by 1 to 2 weeks.
  • Pathologic jaundice: within the first 24 hours, any raised direct fraction, or persistence beyond 2 weeks.
  • Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia: direct bilirubin above 1.0 mg/dL; never physiologic and never breast-milk jaundice.
  • Classic galactosemia: galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency; galactose-1-phosphate accumulates in the liver. Conjugated jaundice, a large liver and a non-glucose reducing sugar in the urine after milk feeds; it predisposes to Escherichia coli sepsis.
  • Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency: indirect jaundice with anemia and Coombs-negative hemolysis, often after an oxidant.
Workup
Causes: timing and the direct fraction
Well or sick, indirect or direct
CauseWhenThe tell
PhysiologicAfter 24 hours, peak day 3 to 5Well infant, feeding and voiding normally; indirect; nothing but time
Suboptimal-intake (breast-feeding) jaundiceDay 3 to 5Weight loss, few wet diapers; feed more often, lactation support
Breast-milk jaundiceDay 7 onward, peak about 2 weeks, can persist weeksThriving, indirect, normal GGT and stools; continue breast-feeding
Blood group or Rh hemolytic diseaseOften within 24 hoursCoombs positive; mother group O or Rh-negative; high reticulocytes
G6PD deficiency Can't missVariable, can be abruptCoombs negative, anemia, high reticulocytes, often an oxidant; X-linked, mostly boys; Mediterranean, African or Asian ancestry; remove the trigger, phototherapy
Biliary atresia Can't missWell at birth; jaundice and hepatomegaly at 2 to 8 weeksDirect, high GGT and ALP, normal reticulocytes; acholic stools, dark urine; reducing substances negative
PFICInfancyDirect with a normal GGT; gallbladder present; specialist evaluation
Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosisInfancy, acuteFebrile and ill; direct and GGT high, cytopenias, low reticulocytes, normal gallbladder; urgent hematology
Crigler-Najjar or GilbertPersistent indirectThe same enzyme absent or reduced, not immature; depends on type
Classic galactosemiaWithin days of milk feedsSick; conjugated jaundice, hepatomegaly, urine reducing substances
Numbers and gates Visible – above about 5 mg/dL · Physiologic ceiling – peak around 14 to 15 mg/dL, indirect over 90% · Exchange range – generally above 20 mg/dL; kernicterus risk rises at 25 to 30 mg/dL · Under 24 hours – never physiologic: bilirubin with a direct fraction and a Coombs · Any direct fraction – not physiologic: consider obstruction or infection · Beyond 2 weeks – check the direct fraction and the stool color before reassuring · Phototherapy versus exchange – phototherapy first; exchange for the severe range or signs of encephalopathy, not a level near threshold · Feeding – almost never a reason to stop breast-feeding; more milk increases bilirubin excretion through the gut
The sick neonate with a positive screen
Galactosemia: act now Stop – all lactose and galactose immediately, without waiting for confirmation, because the injury is ongoing · Feed – soy-based formula in place of breast milk and standard formula · In parallel – blood, urine and cerebrospinal fluid cultures and empiric neonatal antibiotics for Escherichia coli · Confirm afterwards – red cell GALT activity · Urine test – needs recent intake, so a negative test after feeds stop does not exclude galactosemia
Screen-positive and sick: the liver and the urine name it
DiagnosisThe tell
Galactokinase deficiencyCataracts in a well infant; no liver disease, no sepsis
Congenital rubella syndromeCataracts with deafness and a patent ductus arteriosus, blueberry muffin rash; present at birth, not triggered by milk
Hereditary fructose intoleranceAldolase B; same liver picture plus hypoglycemia, at weaning with fruit, juice or sucrose
Maple syrup urine diseaseEncephalopathy without hepatomegaly or cholestasis; sweet-smelling urine, ketosis
Practice
  1. 4-day-old boy born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery is jaundiced breast-feeding without difficulty; eight wet diapers daily alert; Apgar scores 10 and 10 Afebrile · total bilirubin 11 mg/dL → Immature UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity → a well infant, feeding and voiding normally, jaundiced on day 4 at 11 mg/dL has physiologic jaundice: fetal hemoglobin breaks down quickly while the conjugating enzyme is still immature, so unconjugated bilirubin accumulates. Enterohepatic circulation is increased in the newborn, not decreased, and ligandin is low at birth, not high: real mechanisms stated in the wrong direction. Cholestasis would make the bilirubin direct, and albumin displacement needs a displacing drug
  2. 3-day-old girl born at term is seen at a follow-up visit newborn screen reported positive for galactosemia by telephone asymptomatic and breastfeeding well Afebrile · weight 3% below birth weight · no jaundice → Stop breastfeeding and start soy-based formula pending confirmation → presumptive galactosemia: stop all lactose and galactose immediately, without waiting for confirmation, because the injury is ongoing; replace breast milk with soy-based formula and confirm afterwards with red cell GALT activity. Continuing feeds continues the injury, and intravenous antibiotics answer a febrile or septic neonate, not this well one
  3. 4-week-old term boy, well-appearing, has weeks of yellowing of the eyes now jaundiced to the chest; exclusively breastfed stools fewer and paler; soft abdomen, enlarged liver ultrasound shows no visible gallbladder Afebrile · weight 25th percentile · total bilirubin 12.5 mg/dL → Direct bilirubin high, GGT high, reticulocyte count normal → pale stools and an absent gallbladder mean bile duct destruction, which raises the direct fraction and the GGT while the reticulocytes stay normal: biliary atresia. A direct rise with a normal GGT is progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis, and an indirect rise with high reticulocytes is hemolysis. Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis also raises both, but in a febrile, ill infant with low reticulocytes. Exclusive breastfeeding suggests breast-milk jaundice, but that is indirect and leaves the stools yellow and the gallbladder normal. Intraoperative cholangiography confirms, then Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy
  4. 9-month-old girl has vomiting and jaundice began after juice and fruit were introduced liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin urine positive for reducing substances Afebrile · glucose 38 mg/dL → Hereditary fructose intolerance → aldolase B deficiency gives the same hepatic picture as galactosemia plus hypoglycemia, but it starts with fruit, juice or sucrose at weaning, months old rather than days; remove fructose, sucrose and sorbitol. Glycogen storage disease type I brings hypoglycemia within hours of fasting with no dietary trigger; essential fructosuria is the benign cousin, a urinary sugar with no illness
  5. 2-day-old girl born at term has jaundice to the chest infant blood group B, mother group O direct Coombs test positive Alert and breast-feeding well Afebrile · total bilirubin 19 mg/dL · direct 0.6 mg/dL → Phototherapy → a positive Coombs test with a group O mother is isoimmune hemolysis, still below the exchange range. Phototherapy comes first; exchange transfusion is for the severe range (generally above 20 mg/dL) or signs of encephalopathy, not a level near threshold. Jaundice is almost never a reason to stop breast-feeding: more milk increases bilirubin excretion through the gut
  6. 2-week-old girl was diagnosed with classic galactosemia last week parents ask what she can be fed jaundice resolving on her current feeds Mother hopes to resume breastfeeding Afebrile · weight gain 25 g/day → Breast milk → breast milk and standard formula carry lactose, so they are replaced with soy-based formula; the diet reverses the acute illness. An elemental lactose-free formula carries no lactose either
  7. 4-day-old girl born at term is jaundiced exclusively breast-fed weight 11% below birth weight three wet diapers in the past day Examination otherwise normal Afebrile · total bilirubin 14 mg/dL, direct 0.4 mg/dL → Suboptimal-intake jaundice → weight loss and few wet diapers in the first week are a hungry infant: too little milk, not the milk itself, raising bilirubin through increased enterohepatic reabsorption (also called breast-feeding jaundice). Feed more often, with lactation support. Breast-milk jaundice is a thriving infant still jaundiced in the second week, and biliary atresia raises the direct fraction
  8. 10-day-old boy born at term is jaundiced liver edge 4 cm below the costal margin urine positive for reducing substances Newborn screen flagged a disorder of galactose metabolism Afebrile · direct bilirubin 3 mg/dL → Red cell GALT enzyme activity → red cell GALT activity names the enzyme defect: absent or near absent in classic galactosemia, and invalid after transfusion. Reduced red cell GALT activity establishes the diagnosis, and a serum galactose level only supports it
  9. 6-week-old girl born at term has jaundice acholic stools and dark urine liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin exclusively breast-fed; gaining weight Afebrile · total bilirubin 8 mg/dL · direct bilirubin 5 mg/dL → Biliary atresia → a direct fraction is never physiologic, and acholic stools with dark urine at 2 to 8 weeks in an infant well at birth is duct obstruction. An exclusively breastfed infant can still have it: breast-milk jaundice is indirect, peaks around 2 weeks and leaves the stools yellow. Physiologic jaundice is predominantly indirect and resolves by 1 to 2 weeks
  10. 5-day-old boy born at term has poor feeding and lethargy seizures today urine smells like maple syrup Newborn screen reported positive T 36.9 °C · glucose 72 mg/dL · no hepatomegaly or jaundice → Leucine-free formula with dextrose → branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency (signs from day 2 to 3) is encephalopathy without hepatomegaly or cholestasis, with sweet-smelling urine and ketosis: the right class of screen-flagged inborn error to confuse with galactosemia, but it carries ketoacids, not a reducing sugar. Soy formula, the galactosemia substitute, still contains protein, including the branched-chain amino acids, so it keeps feeding the block; protein is given as amino acids free of the branched chains, with isoleucine and valine added back, so the formula is leucine-free, and high calories come as dextrose and lipid. Antibiotics with observation do not lower plasma leucine
  11. 5-day-old boy born at term is jaundiced to the abdomen breast-feeding poorly with few wet diapers dry mucous membranes; weight 10% below birth weight Afebrile · total bilirubin 16 mg/dL · direct 0.5 mg/dL → Increased enterohepatic reabsorption → the newborn gut reabsorbs bilirubin, so anything that slows transit raises the indirect fraction: too little milk slows it and lets intestinal bilirubin return to the circulation. Conjugation is immature in every newborn, and albumin displacement requires a displacing drug
  12. 10-day-old girl born at term vomits after starting formula jaundiced, with the liver 4 cm below the costal margin bilateral cataracts urine positive for reducing substances Afebrile · direct bilirubin 3 mg/dL → Classic galactosemia → conjugated jaundice with hepatomegaly, cataracts and urine reducing substances within days of milk feeds: liver, kidney, brain and lens are affected; eliminate galactose and lactose. Glycogen storage disease type I has no galactose trigger and no cataracts; hereditary fructose intolerance appears at weaning
  13. 14-hour-old boy born at term has visible jaundice of the face and chest breast-feeding well Uncomplicated pregnancy and vaginal delivery; examination otherwise normal Afebrile · HR 140/min · transcutaneous bilirubin 9 mg/dL → Total and direct bilirubin with a Coombs test → onset inside 24 hours is never physiologic, so it is pathologic until proven otherwise: send bilirubin with a direct fraction and a Coombs test. Hepatic ultrasound and serum albumin cannot show hemolysis or immature conjugation
  14. 3-week-old girl was diagnosed with classic galactosemia at 1 week bilateral cataracts seen on red reflex examination on soy formula; jaundice resolving Liver edge now 1 cm below the costal margin Afebrile · weight gain 30 g/day → Galactitol accumulation via aldose reductase → cataracts in both galactose disorders come from galactitol, made by aldose reductase, the same enzyme that makes sorbitol in the diabetic lens: an osmotic lens injury. Galactokinase deficiency makes cataracts without ever forming galactose-1-phosphate, so the lens injury is galactitol, not galactose-1-phosphate; sorbitol is the diabetic product
  15. 4-day-old term boy of Greek descent is jaundiced to the abdomen feeding well Mother and infant both group A, Rh-positive direct Coombs negative; no spherocytes on smear hematocrit 36% · reticulocytes high · bilirubin 17 mg/dL, direct 0.6 mg/dL → G6PD enzyme activity level → Coombs-negative hemolysis (anemia with high reticulocytes) in a boy of Mediterranean ancestry is G6PD deficiency: X-linked, so mostly boys, and often an oxidant trigger. Osmotic fragility testing looks for spherocytosis, which the smear argues against, and a liver panel answers a raised direct fraction
  16. 8-day-old boy born at term is jaundiced vomits after breastfeeds liver edge 4 cm below the costal margin urine positive for reducing substances, dipstick glucose negative Afebrile · direct bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL → Stop breast milk and start soy-based formula → a conjugated fraction, a large liver and a non-glucose reducing sugar after days of milk feeds indicate classic galactosemia: stop breast milk now and start soy formula. Phototherapy treats an indirect rise, and continuing feeds continues the injury; the diet reverses the liver disease, so transplant evaluation is not the step
  17. 3-day-old boy born at term is jaundiced to the chest a sulfonamide is proposed for a suspected urinary tract infection Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity is normal Afebrile · total bilirubin 15 mg/dL · direct 0.5 mg/dL → Displacement of bilirubin from albumin → free bilirubin crosses into the basal ganglia. Sulfonamides and ceftriaxone displace bilirubin from albumin, so they are avoided in jaundiced newborns; when G6PD is deficient a sulfonamide also causes hemolysis, a second way it harms, excluded here by the normal enzyme.
  18. 6-week-old boy born at term is well and growing bilateral cataracts on red reflex examination no hepatomegaly; no jaundice urine positive for reducing substances Passed newborn hearing screen; no murmur Afebrile · weight at the 50th percentile → Galactokinase deficiency → a block one step earlier diverts galactose to galactitol: cataracts in a well infant, with no liver disease and no sepsis; lactose-free diet. Classic galactosemia traps toxic galactose-1-phosphate and makes the whole sick-neonate picture; congenital rubella brings cataracts with deafness and a patent ductus arteriosus, present at birth and not triggered by milk
  19. 4-week-old boy born at term is well and feeding well jaundiced, with acholic stools urine negative for reducing substances Afebrile · weight at the 40th percentile · total bilirubin 7 mg/dL · direct bilirubin 5 mg/dL → Abdominal ultrasound and HIDA scan → a direct fraction in a well infant with acholic stools and negative reducing substances is biliary atresia: image first, then intraoperative cholangiogram confirms, and Kasai follows confirmation, before about 60 days. Phototherapy treats an indirect rise
  20. 3-day-old boy, formula-fed, has increasing lethargy and vomiting breathing rapidly; no jaundice, no hepatomegaly, clear lenses Urine negative for reducing substances Afebrile · arterial pH 7.50, low carbon dioxide · ammonia markedly elevated · glucose 80 mg/dL → Urea cycle disorder → very high ammonia with lethargy and respiratory alkalosis in the first days of feeding, with no jaundice, hepatomegaly or cataracts: hyperammonemia; stop protein and lower the ammonia. Classic galactosemia brings conjugated jaundice, hepatomegaly and urine reducing sugar; maple syrup urine disease brings sweet-smelling urine and ketosis
  21. 4-day-old girl born at term is jaundiced exclusively breast-fed; weight 9% below birth weight only three wet diapers today; alert and well Afebrile · total bilirubin 14 mg/dL · direct 0.4 mg/dL → Stopping breast-feeding → this is suboptimal intake, and jaundice is almost never a reason to stop breast-feeding: feed more often, not less, because milk intake drives bilirubin out through the gut. Lactation support with more frequent feeds, and phototherapy if the level crosses threshold, are both appropriate
  22. 3-month-old boy has a protuberant abdomen and doll-like facies massive hepatomegaly hypoglycemia after a 4-hour fast No cataracts; urine negative for reducing substances Afebrile · lactate 6 mmol/L · triglycerides 450 mg/dL · glucose 35 mg/dL → Glycogen storage disease type I → hepatomegaly with fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis and hypertriglyceridemia, with hypoglycemia within hours of fasting, no galactose trigger and no cataracts; treat with frequent cornstarch feeds. Galactosemia needs milk feeds and urine reducing sugar; hereditary fructose intolerance starts with fruit or sucrose at weaning
  23. 6-week-old boy born at term, jaundiced since 3 weeks of age clay-colored stools, dark urine ultrasound: small gallbladder, triangular cord sign intraoperative cholangiogram: no contrast reaches the duodenum Afebrile · direct bilirubin 6 mg/dL · GGT high → Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy → no contrast reaching the bowel confirms biliary atresia: Kasai before about 60 days, best done early, and most eventually need a liver transplant, so transplant is the later step, not the first. Ursodeoxycholic acid is given after the Kasai, not in place of it
  24. 12-day-old girl was diagnosed with galactosemia on day 6 on soy formula since diagnosis now lethargic and feeding poorly Jaundice improving; liver smaller T 38.8 °C · HR 186/min · capillary refill 3 seconds → Blood, urine and CSF cultures, then IV ampicillin and gentamicin → galactosemia predisposes to Escherichia coli sepsis, and a neonate with suspected sepsis gets a lumbar puncture once able to tolerate it: culture blood, urine and cerebrospinal fluid, then start empiric neonatal antibiotics. Ceftriaxone displaces bilirubin from albumin, so it is avoided in a jaundiced newborn, and observing off antibiotics leaves the infection untreated
  25. 3-week-old girl born at term is still jaundiced to the chest exclusively breastfed and gaining weight well yellow stools and pale urine Seen at a routine visit; examination otherwise normal Afebrile → Serum total and direct bilirubin → jaundice past 2 weeks needs a direct fraction, and the stool color, before reassurance; an indirect result in a thriving infant is breast-milk jaundice. A transcutaneous reading gives no direct fraction, and a Coombs test answers jaundice inside 24 hours, not prolonged jaundice
  26. 9-day-old breastfed girl has 3 days of vomiting and poor feeding jaundiced; liver 4 cm below the costal margin bilateral cataracts Normal hearing screen, no murmur; mother 39, declined vaccines T 38.4 °C · blood culture: Escherichia coli → Inability to metabolize galactose in breast milk → a milk-fed neonate with conjugated jaundice, a large liver, cataracts and Escherichia coli sepsis has classic galactosemia: stop breast milk and start soy formula without waiting for confirmation, and treat the sepsis in parallel. Congenital rubella, the vaccine decoy, brings cataracts with deafness and a patent ductus arteriosus, present at birth; a normal hearing screen and no murmur argue against it. Classic galactosemia is autosomal recessive, so the mother's age is a decoy
  27. 2-year-old girl was diagnosed with classic galactosemia on newborn screening fed soy formula since day 5 parents ask about her long-term outlook Afebrile · height and weight at the 50th percentile → Speech and learning problems and ovarian insufficiency can occur despite the diet → even with an early, strict diet, children can have cognitive deficits and speech problems (verbal dyspraxia), and girls develop primary ovarian insufficiency. The diet reverses the acute liver, sepsis and cataract illness but does not prevent these, so normal fertility is not expected, and neither is progressive cirrhosis
  28. 3-week-old boy born at term is still jaundiced at a weight check exclusively breast-fed and gaining weight well yellow stools; thriving Examination otherwise normal Afebrile · total bilirubin 13 mg/dL · direct 0.5 mg/dL → Breast-milk jaundice → milk beta-glucuronidase deconjugates bilirubin and increases enterohepatic circulation: from day 7, peaking around 2 weeks and able to persist for weeks, in a thriving infant with normal stools; continue breast-feeding. Suboptimal intake is a hungry infant losing weight in the first week, and biliary atresia raises the direct fraction and turns the stools pale
How NBME framed it: question 1

5-day-old boy of Mediterranean descent with 2 days of progressive jaundice Five yellow, seedy stools a day; 2 ounces of cow's milk formula every 2 hours Born at term to a 32-year-old primigravida, who took an old sulfamethoxazole prescription for cystitis in the third trimester Mother and infant both group O, Rh-positive examination normal except jaundice from the head to the upper thighs hematocrit 33% · total bilirubin 20 mg/dL, direct 0.9 mg/dL direct and indirect Coombs tests negative

Most likely explanation for the jaundice?

Competing answers
  • Dehydration: raises indirect bilirubin through enterohepatic reabsorption; but feeds every 2 hours and five stools a day argue against it, and it does not cause anemia.
  • Sepsis: can raise indirect bilirubin; but he is well on examination, and Coombs-negative anemia after an oxidant exposure points to hemolysis.
  • Milk protein allergy: the cow's milk formula is the decoy; allergy causes reflux, enterocolitis, enteropathy or urticaria, not hemolysis.

Down to two: enzyme deficiency or physiologic jaundice. Enzyme deficiency: a total of 20 mg/dL exceeds the physiologic peak of about 15, and a hematocrit of 33% points to hemolysis. A negative Coombs removes isoimmune hemolysis; Mediterranean ancestry and a maternal sulfonamide point to G6PD deficiency. G6PD makes NADPH (reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate), which keeps glutathione reduced; without it, sulfonamides and other oxidants cause hemolysis. The key named only the class.

Read three labs together Direct high, GGT high, reticulocytes normal – duct obstruction: biliary atresia in a well infant with pale stools · Direct high, GGT normal – progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis · Direct and GGT high, reticulocytes low, cytopenias – hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis in a febrile, ill infant · Indirect, reticulocytes high – hemolysis · Indirect, everything else normal – breast-milk jaundice in a thriving infant; an exclusively breastfed infant can still have biliary atresia, so pale stools and a direct fraction decide it
The galactose pathway Reducing substances positive with dipstick glucose negative means galactose or fructose, because glucose is itself a reducing sugar, so read both tests. Galactokinase makes galactose-1-phosphate, and GALT converts it to uridine diphosphate galactose and glucose-1-phosphate. A galactokinase block leaves only galactitol, so cataracts alone; a GALT block traps toxic galactose-1-phosphate, so the whole sick-neonate picture, affecting liver, kidney, brain and lens. Cataracts in both come from galactitol via aldose reductase, the enzyme that makes sorbitol in the diabetic lens. Even with an early, strict diet, children can have cognitive deficits and speech problems, and girls develop primary ovarian insufficiency.
Common wrong answers Ligandin or enterohepatic circulation: real mechanisms stated in the wrong direction (ligandin is low and enterohepatic circulation increased in the newborn). Exchange transfusion at a level still in the phototherapy range. Maple syrup urine disease for a sick jaundiced neonate: the right class of screen-flagged inborn error, but no hepatomegaly, and ketoacids rather than a reducing sugar. Cystic fibrosis because the screen is positive: screened by immunoreactive trypsinogen, it presents with meconium ileus or quiet cholestasis, not fever with urinary sugar. Sickle cell or neonatal hyperthyroidism: screen-positive with no hepatic picture; sickle cell jaundice is unconjugated and silent at 10 days because fetal hemoglobin protects. Urea cycle disorder: very high ammonia with lethargy and respiratory alkalosis, but no jaundice, hepatomegaly or cataracts. Glycogen storage disease type I: hypoglycemia within hours of fasting with lactic acidosis, but no galactose trigger and no cataracts. Sulfonamides and ceftriaxone displace bilirubin from albumin, and a sulfonamide also causes hemolysis when G6PD is deficient.
Exam answer versus current evidence Board questions use 60 days as the Kasai cutoff, and the Kasai is ideally done before 60 days. The evidence shows no sharp cutoff: native-liver survival falls continuously with age at operation, and a 2023 meta-analysis found operating at 30 days or earlier still better than at 31 to 60 days. Use 60 days as the exam threshold, not as a deadline with room to spare.
Pairs with Part I Abnormal Liver Tests: the conjugated-versus-unconjugated workup in adults. Hereditary fructose intolerance has no brief of its own: did symptoms start with fruit or sucrose? Biliary atresia: is the infant sick or well, and are reducing substances present? Part I Congenital Hypothyroidism: another positive newborn screen, where the thyroid-stimulating hormone level and the neck locate the defect; in galactosemia, the enzyme deficiency and the organism locate it.
Transferable rule

When every option names a real mechanism, check which direction each one moves in this patient before choosing. A positive newborn screen never names the disease when every disorder under consideration is on the panel: the bilirubin fraction, the liver and the urine identify it, and a febrile neonate is cultured and treated for sepsis in parallel with the metabolic diagnosis, not after it.

Maternal Effects in the Newborn

maternal creatinine, antibodies and hormones · carryover or the baby's own disease · what is physiologic and what is notIs the infant well and inside the window, and does the mother's chart explain the finding?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

In the first days a newborn's value or finding can be the mother's. Read her chart first.

  • Creatinine: crosses the placenta; the day-1 value is the mother's.
  • IgG (immunoglobulin G) antibodies: cross and cause disease, mostly transient (heart block is permanent); IgM (immunoglobulin M) and TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) do not cross.
  • Estrogen: withdrawal bleeding, leukorrhea, labial swelling, breast hypertrophy with or without galactorrhea.

When a value disagrees with urine output, growth and exam, those decide. Reassure only on positive criteria, and only after checking for each disqualifying finding.

Diagnosis
Kidneys working Output – at least one void per day of life; none by 24 hours is abnormal · Weight – loss under 10% in the first days; beyond that, look for feeding failure with hypernatremia and prerenal azotemia · Red flags – oliguria, edema, hypertension, or a risk factor: ultrasound and trended creatinine; risk factors: a nephrotoxic drug (gentamicin) or perinatal hypoxia
The baby's own kidney Bilateral renal agenesis – no or minimal urine, respiratory distress, Potter facies, limb deformities · Hypoxic-ischemic injury – low Apgars, abnormal neurologic exam; creatinine rises over days · Dehydration – loss of 10% or more with fewer voids; breastfeeding jaundice reaches creatinine only this way
Maternal antibodies Anti-Ro/SSA – with maternal SLE (systemic lupus erythematosus) or no overt autoimmune disease, with fetal or neonatal bradycardia: congenital heart block · Graves – TSI (thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin), neonatal thyrotoxicosis · ITP (immune thrombocytopenia) – antiplatelet IgG, neonatal thrombocytopenia; thyrotoxicosis and thrombocytopenia usually resolve as maternal IgG clears; complete heart block is permanent
Hormone withdrawal Mechanism – maternal estrogen proliferates the fetal endometrium; at delivery progesterone is withdrawn and estrogen support is lost; the lining sloughs · Window – light bleeding in the first 2 weeks, lasting under 5 days, in a well infant
Not physiologic Candida – thick, adherent discharge, red mucosa; bleeding atypical; uncommon without a risk factor (diapers, recent antibiotics, diabetes or immunosuppression) · Group A Streptococcus – purulent, not bloody; red mucosa; household contact; uncommon · Foreign body – toilet-training age or self-exploration, odor, pain · Vertical chlamydia – conjunctivitis in the first weeks or afebrile pneumonia at 4 to 12 weeks · Mastitis – unilateral red, warm, tender bud; systemic signs uncommon · Abuse – bleeding outside the window, an inconsistent history, other injuries, or an STI (sexually transmitted infection) organism after the newborn period; evaluation until proven otherwise
Management and treatment
Management ladder: a high newborn creatinine
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Well, output and exam normal, maternal source: document voids, repeat the creatinineFewer voids than days of life, edema, hypertension, no fall
2Red flag or risk factor (nephrotoxic drug, perinatal hypoxia): renal ultrasound, trended creatinine, medication reviewAnuria, rising creatinine, electrolyte or fluid derangement
3Nephrology; renal replacement therapy if refractoryTop rung
By diagnosis Hormone effects – clinical diagnosis; reassurance; nothing cultured or imaged · Mastitis – culture and antibiotics · Abuse concern – evaluation, never reassurance
Practice
  1. 23-hour-old girl, well appearing, has jaundice 2 voids, 3% weight loss Apgars 8 and 9; no edema Born by cesarean after arrest of labor Mother on hemodialysis for end-stage renal disease Normotensive · total bilirubin 4.3 mg/dL · creatinine 4.2 mg/dL → Maternal creatinine carryover → creatinine crosses the placenta, so the day-1 value is the mother's; voids, weight, Apgars and exam show the kidneys work
  2. 1-day-old girl, well appearing, has voided twice 2% weight loss, normal examination Newborn of a mother on hemodialysis for end-stage renal disease Normotensive · serum creatinine 4.2 mg/dL on day 1 → Repeat serum creatinine in 1-2 weeks → the value falls over 2 weeks to a nadir set by the infant's own muscle mass; that later value is the baby's
  3. 23-hour-old boy, well appearing, is voiding normally 3% weight loss, normal examination Mother on hemodialysis for end-stage renal disease His creatinine is explained by the maternal disease Normotensive · creatinine 4.2 mg/dL → Initiate neonatal renal replacement therapy → the number is not the infant's: document voids and repeat it; replacement therapy treats a kidney that is working
  4. 4-day-old boy is rechecked in the nursery creatinine still 4.2 mg/dL, unchanged since day 1 one void in 24 hours Mother on hemodialysis for end-stage renal disease Afebrile · weight 6% below birth weight → Renal ultrasound and a trended creatinine → the value should have been falling, and fewer voids than days of life is oliguria: it points to the baby's own kidney
  5. 1-day-old boy has respiratory distress no void in 26 hours flat facies and limb deformities Bladder not palpable; no urine on catheterization respiratory rate 72/min · oxygen saturation 88% on room air → Bilateral renal agenesis → Potter sequence from oligohydramnios: no or minimal urine, pulmonary hypoplasia, flat facies and limb deformities; image now
  6. 4-hour-old term boy is lethargic and hypotonic Apgar scores 2 and 4 cord pH 6.9 Delivered after a prolonged second stage of labor; resuscitated in the delivery room T 36.9 °C · HR 150/min · no seizures → Therapeutic hypothermia → start within 6 hours; asphyxia injures the tubules, so the creatinine rises over days: supportive renal care
  7. 5-day-old girl who is breastfeeding is sleepy and feeding poorly 12% weight loss since birth one void in 24 hours; sunken fontanelle Feeds are short and infrequent Afebrile · sodium 152 mEq/L · urea nitrogen 40 mg/dL → Supervised feeding with supplementation and rehydration → over 10% loss with hypernatremia and a raised urea nitrogen is breastfeeding failure with prerenal azotemia
  8. 3-day-old boy, well appearing, has a low platelet count on screening no petechiae, bruising or bleeding feeding well after a term vaginal delivery Mother has immune thrombocytopenia Afebrile · platelets 70,000/mm³ · normal neurologic examination → Observe with serial platelet counts → transplacental antiplatelet IgG; a well infant without bleeding is observed while the maternal antibody clears
  9. 5-day-old girl is irritable and tachycardic at a follow-up visit a goiter is palpable Mother has Graves disease Delivered at term; feeding every 2 to 3 hours T 37.6 °C · HR 205/min · weight 2% below birth weight → Methimazole with a beta-blocker → transplacental thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin; HR 205 with irritability is thyrotoxicosis that needs treatment now, even though it usually clears with the maternal antibody
  10. 1-day-old boy has a heart rate of 55/min fetal heart rate 55/min at 22 weeks persisting after birth at term Mother has systemic lupus erythematosus Afebrile · no murmur · pink and well perfused → Maternal anti-Ro/SSA antibody transfer → transplacental passage causes congenital complete heart block; one line of maternal history names it
  11. 5-day-old girl has white mucoid vaginal discharge streaked with blood feeding and voiding well; no odor or mucosal redness Exclusively breastfed Forceps-assisted delivery; a 9-year-old sister at home Afebrile · otherwise normal examination → Maternal hormone withdrawal → physiologic and self-limited; a forceps delivery does not bleed 5 days later; a sibling's group A streptococcus would cause purulent discharge; candida brings a thick, adherent discharge on an erythematous mucosa, and a foreign body needs toilet-training age
  12. 5-day-old girl, well appearing, has vaginal discharge white and mucoid, streaked with blood Her mother was treated for an STI early in pregnancy, then tested negative Her parents ask for testing Afebrile · normal examination → Reassurance and observation → the diagnosis is clinical and resolves within days; the mother's negative test after treatment closes the vertical branch
  13. 4-day-old girl has light vaginal bleeding labial swelling and bilateral breast buds white vaginal discharge, no odor No bleeding from the cord or puncture sites; feeding well Afebrile · well appearing · otherwise normal examination → Progesterone withdrawal after delivery → maternal estrogen proliferates the fetal endometrium in utero; after delivery progesterone is withdrawn and estrogen support is lost, so the lining sloughs
  14. 3-week-old boy has bilateral breast enlargement a drop of milky fluid from each nipple no redness or tenderness Feeding well and gaining weight since birth Afebrile · no fluctuance · otherwise normal examination → Physiologic breast hypertrophy → breast hypertrophy with galactorrhea is another maternal estrogen effect
  15. 2-week-old girl has irritability a red, warm, tender breast bud on one side feeding less over the past day Breast enlargement had been noted at birth T 38.5 °C · HR 180/min → Culture and intravenous antibiotics → neonatal mastitis: a unilateral red, warm, tender bud is not physiologic hypertrophy
  16. 10-day-old girl, well appearing, is brought in by her parents vaginal bleeding has continued 8 days bleeding is increasing at day 10 of life Feeding and voiding well; no bruising elsewhere Afebrile · otherwise normal examination → Evaluate further rather than reassure → outside the self-limited window: physiologic bleeding lasts under 5 days
  17. 4-year-old girl, toilet trained, has had 1 week of vaginal discharge foul-smelling and bloody pain with wiping No systemic symptoms; no vomiting or abdominal pain Afebrile · no rash · well appearing → Examination for a vaginal foreign body → toilet paper is the commonest; it needs toilet-training age or self-exploration, plus odor and pain
  18. 6-year-old girl is brought in with vaginal discharge for 1 week positive gonorrhea nucleic acid amplification test Her mother asks whether a shared towel could explain it Afebrile · well appearing · no other findings on examination → Report for suspected sexual abuse → report and initiate an evaluation: a sexually transmitted organism outside the newborn period is never a reassurance branch
  19. 6-week-old boy has an afebrile staccato cough tachypnea without wheeze or fever had purulent conjunctivitis as a 7-day-old Mother untreated for an STI in pregnancy T 37.1 °C · respiratory rate 64/min → Vertical Chlamydia trachomatis transmission → vertical chlamydia: eyes and lungs
Decoys Bilirubin: why the panel was drawn; it does not explain the creatinine. Arrest of labor, cesarean: suggest an insult; normal Apgars counter it. White, a maternal STI, blood streaks, a sibling, forceps: point to candida, chlamydia, a foreign body, streptococcus, trauma; age and wellness answer each. A negative test after treatment closes the infectious branch.
Pairs with Posterior Urethral Valves: the oliguric end, where the creatinine is the baby's. Rashes in the Newborn and Infant: the same sort for skin: physiologic, removable or pathologic.
Transferable rule

A newborn finding can be the mother's. Read her chart with the panel, let output, growth and exam decide, and reassure only on positive criteria, and only after checking for each disqualifying finding: fever, pain, odor, purulence, systemic illness, or a finding outside its window.

Diabetes Complications and Annual Care

the annual care bundle and the outcome noun · kidney screening by detection threshold · foot ulcers read by exam, not risk profileIs the outcome morbidity, mortality, hospitalization or benefit, which test catches the reversible stage, and does the exam overrule the risk profile?

Annual careKidneyFootPractice
Bottom line

Read the outcome noun before the options.

  • Morbidity: disease burden (complications and disability), so preventing it in diabetes means screening for a complication.
  • Mortality: death.
  • Dilated eye exam: finds retinopathy, the most common preventable complication; asymptomatic until advanced, and the leading cause of new blindness in working-age adults.
  • Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR): the kidney screen, because the most sensitive test has the lowest detection threshold. It detects 30 to 300 mg/g, the reversible window; the dipstick turns positive only at about 300 mg/day or more and depends on urine concentration.
  • Persistent albuminuria: with hypertension, if not pregnant, an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB); in type 2 diabetes with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 20 mL/min/1.73 m² or more, add a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor; never an ACE inhibitor with an ARB.
  • Hyperfiltration: early nephropathy can keep creatinine normal or low while glomeruli are lost, so a normal creatinine does not exclude early diabetic kidney disease.
  • Neuropathic ulcer: painless, plantar over a bony prominence, on a warm foot. Together these point away from arterial disease, but neuropathy hides ischemic pain, so pulses and an ankle-brachial index (ABI) are still checked: a normal ABI, with a normal toe-brachial index, makes arterial disease less likely but cannot exclude it, since calcified vessels raise the ABI. Warm means perfused; dry means autonomic denervation. Diabetes is the most common cause.
  • Three tests, three questions: a culture characterizes the wound, the ABI the perfusion; only the hemoglobin A1c identifies the underlying disease.
Annual care
The annual bundle Dilated eye exam – yearly, or every 1 to 2 years may be considered after normal exams with well-controlled glycemia; first exam at diagnosis in type 2, within 5 years of onset in adult type 1; macular edema, moderate or worse nonproliferative, or any proliferative retinopathy to ophthalmology · Monofilament foot exam – yearly; lost protective sensation means neuropathy: foot care education, podiatry, inspect the feet each visit · UACR with serum creatinine – yearly · Blood pressure – every visit · Lipids – at least every 5 years · Counseling – depression screening; weight and tobacco counseling · A1c – every 3 months if not at goal or after a therapy change; every 6 months when stable at goal · Pneumococcal vaccine – diabetes is a risk-based indication in adults 19 to 49; every adult 50 or older is vaccinated by age (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)
Outcome word → intervention selected
The stem asksIt meansIt selects
Prevent morbidityComplications, disabilityScreening for the complication
Reduce mortalityDeathInterventions with survival data (long-term oxygen in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease)
Reduce hospitalizationAdmissionsThe driver of decompensation (blood pressure control in heart failure)
Most beneficialMagnitude, any outcomeUsually smoking cessation
Kidney
Albuminuria screening schedule
