Type 1 diabetes5 years after diagnosisYearly
Hypertension, chronic kidney disease, lupus, sickle cell disease, human immunodeficiency virus infection, nephrotoxic drugsAt diagnosisYearly or by risk
Healthy asymptomatic adultUS Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF): no recommendation (I statement), insufficient evidenceNone
Other question verbs Quantify total protein – when a non-albumin protein is suspected: urine protein-to-creatinine ratio or 24-hour protein; dipstick and UACR miss light chains (myeloma: dipstick negative, sulfosalicylic acid test positive, urine protein electrophoresis shows an M-spike) · Most accurate glomerular filtration rate (GFR) – measured clearance (inulin or iothalamate); cystatin C when creatinine is unreliable (amputees, cachexia, bodybuilders, cirrhosis)
Biopsy triggers: atypical for diabetic nephropathy No retinopathy · active sediment (dysmorphic red cells, red cell casts) · rapid GFR decline · nephrotic-range proteinuria too early · diabetes duration too short.
Foot
Leg and foot ulcer types
TypeSite and painBed, skin, pulses, test
Neuropathic (diabetic)Plantar pressure points (first or fifth metatarsal head, heel); painlessPunched out, necrotic base, surrounding callus; warm, dry, fissured skin; pulses normal; A1c, 10-g monofilament
Arterial (ischemic)Toe tips, lateral malleolus, dorsum; painful, worse elevated, better danglingDry, pale, little granulation; cool, shiny, hairless skin, dependent rubor; pulses weak or absent; ABI
Venous stasisMedial malleolus (gaiter area); mild ache, better elevatedShallow, irregular, wet; hemosiderin staining, edema; pulses normal; duplex ultrasound, then compression

ABI bands (American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association) and neuropathy ABI over 1.4 – noncompressible, calcified vessels (diabetes, end-stage renal disease): use the toe-brachial index, abnormal at 0.7 or less · 1.0 to 1.4 – normal · 0.91 to 0.99 – borderline · 0.90 or less – abnormal · 0.5 to 0.9 – claudication · Under 0.4 – critical limb ischemia · Small-fiber neuropathy – pain, burning, autonomic dysfunction · Large-fiber neuropathy – sensory loss, which lets injury go unrecognized · Timing – peripheral neuropathy can be present when type 2 diabetes is diagnosed
Practice
  1. 28-year-old woman had type 2 diabetes diagnosed 1 month ago Asymptomatic; walks daily and has cut out sugary drinks takes metformin; no other medical history BP 122/78 mm Hg · A1c 6.1% → Annual dilated eye exam → morbidity means the complications of diabetes, so the answer screens for one: the dilated eye exam finds retinopathy while it is still asymptomatic. Pneumococcal vaccination is indicated too, but it addresses infection risk downstream of diabetes; monthly A1c measures overlapping windows
  2. 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 6 years Due for his annual kidney screening; feels well takes metformin; no edema BP 128/80 mm Hg · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL · A1c 7.4% → Spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio → the most sensitive test has the lowest detection threshold: the ratio detects 30 to 300 mg/g, the reversible stage. The dipstick stays negative until about 300 mg/day; a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio or 24-hour collection quantifies total protein when a non-albumin protein is suspected
  3. 45-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has had a foot ulcer for 3 weeks painless plantar ulcer over the first metatarsal head surrounding callus; foot warm and dry T 36.9 °C · pedal pulses normal · A1c 9.1% → Neuropathic ulcer → painless, plantar over a bony prominence and warm point away from arterial disease; normal pulses support a perfused foot, but neuropathy hides ischemic pain, so the ABI is still checked, and even a normal ABI and toe-brachial index only make arterial disease less likely; dry skin is autonomic denervation. Off-loading with a total contact cast is the single most important treatment, with debridement and glycemic control
  4. 56-year-old man has type 2 diabetes diagnosed today Thirst and frequent urination for 2 months no medical care in the past 10 years BP 134/84 mm Hg · A1c 8.2% · creatinine 0.8 mg/dL → At diagnosis → in type 2 diabetes kidney screening starts at diagnosis and repeats yearly, because silent hyperglycemia predates the diagnosis by years; in type 1 it starts 5 years after diagnosis
  5. 28-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 2 years asks about A1c frequency A1c at goal on her last three checks No change in her metformin dose for a year BP 118/76 mm Hg · A1c 6.4% → Check the A1c every 6 months → stable at goal means every 6 months; every 3 months is for an A1c not at goal or after a therapy change. Monthly values measure overlapping windows of the 90 to 120 day red cell lifespan
  6. 68-year-old man has had a painful ulcer at the toe tips for 1 month pain worse with the leg raised, better dangling cool pale foot; shiny, hairless skin T 36.8 °C · BP 148/86 mm Hg · absent pulses → Arterial ischemic ulcer → a painful ulcer at the toe tips on a cool, pale, pulseless foot is arterial: confirm with the ankle-brachial index. A neuropathic ulcer is painless and plantar on a warm foot; a venous ulcer is wet and sits at the medial malleolus
  7. 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has a single abnormal albumin-to-creatinine ratio ratio 64 mg/g on his annual screen Ran a 10K race the day before the sample BP 126/78 mm Hg · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL → Repeat the albumin-to-creatinine ratio → confirmation requires 2 of 3 abnormal samples over 3 to 6 months, which excludes transient albuminuria from exercise, fever, infection, heart failure or hyperglycemia; drug treatment starts once it persists
  8. 28-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is due for vaccines Receives this season's influenza vaccine today no asplenia; no chronic lung or heart disease Does not smoke BP 120/76 mm Hg · A1c 6.8% → Pneumococcal vaccination → diabetes is a risk-based indication for pneumococcal vaccination in adults 19 to 49, and every adult 50 or older is vaccinated by age; asplenia is not required
  9. 70-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 25 years is seen for his annual foot exam ABI 1.5 in both legs radiograph shows calcified tibial arteries BP 138/80 mm Hg · creatinine 1.1 mg/dL → Noncompressible vessels → an index over 1.4 means calcified, noncompressible vessels, as in diabetes and end-stage renal disease; the next test is the toe-brachial index, abnormal at 0.7 or less, which can unmask arterial disease the ABI hides
  10. 24-year-old woman has type 1 diabetes diagnosed at 16 Establishing care at a new clinic after a move uses an insulin pump; no kidney screening on record BP 112/70 mm Hg · A1c 7.3% → 5 years after diagnosis → in type 1 diabetes kidney screening starts 5 years after diagnosis, then yearly; it starts at diagnosis only in type 2, where hyperglycemia has been silent for years
  11. 55-year-old man with type 2 diabetes asks what most reduces his risk of death smokes one pack of cigarettes daily Overdue for his eye and foot exams BP 136/84 mm Hg · A1c 7.0% → Smoking cessation → mortality means death, so choose the intervention with survival data: smoking cessation, then blood pressure control and a statin. The eye and foot exams prevent morbidity, not death
  12. 62-year-old woman has had a leg ulcer for 2 months shallow, wet ulcer at the medial malleolus brown hemosiderin staining and ankle edema Mild ache, better with the leg raised T 36.8 °C · pedal pulses normal → Venous stasis ulcer → a shallow, wet ulcer at the medial malleolus with hemosiderin and edema is venous stasis: duplex ultrasound, then compression
  13. 60-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 9 years albumin-to-creatinine ratio 85 mg/g second elevated value in 4 months; the first was 72 mg/g BP 134/82 mm Hg (similar at her last visit) · A1c 7.1% · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL → ACE inhibitor or ARB + SGLT2 inhibitor → persistent albuminuria (2 of 3 samples elevated over 3 to 6 months) with a blood pressure above the American Diabetes Association target of under 130/80 mm Hg calls for an ACE inhibitor or ARB, and in type 2 diabetes with an eGFR of 20 or more an SGLT2 inhibitor as well; a creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL puts her eGFR well above 20. Together they are most likely to slow progression
  14. 61-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has a foot ulcer that has not healed in 2 months plantar foot ulcer over a bony prominence; probe-to-bone test positive Foot radiograph normal T 37.2 °C · ESR 88 mm/h → Osteomyelitis → a probe that touches bone makes osteomyelitis likely, and an ESR over 70 supports it; plain films are insensitive early, so MRI comes next, then bone biopsy, which names the organism
  15. 28-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes asks when to recheck her A1c A1c 9.4% after adding a second agent Takes metformin and sitagliptin; no low blood sugars BP 124/78 mm Hg · weight 82 kg → Check the A1c every 3 months → an A1c not at goal and a therapy change each mean every 3 months; every 6 months is for an A1c stable at goal
  16. 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is enrolling in a drug study below-knee amputation of the right leg last year The study protocol needs an exact filtration rate before dosing BP 130/80 mm Hg · creatinine 0.7 mg/dL → Inulin or iothalamate clearance → measured clearance is the most accurate; creatinine is unreliable in amputees, cachexia, bodybuilders and cirrhosis, where cystatin C helps
  17. 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has a warm, swollen, erythematous right foot swelling for 3 weeks no ulcer or break in the skin; no fever Cannot feel the monofilament on either foot T 36.9 °C · white cells 7,400/mm³ → Charcot arthropathy → a warm, swollen, red foot with no ulcer, fever or raised white count in a diabetic with peripheral neuropathy suggests Charcot arthropathy (confirm with radiographs or MRI): immobilize; rocker-bottom deformity
  18. 32-year-old woman has type 1 diabetes diagnosed at age 26 Establishing care after a move; old records lost reports she has never had a dilated eye examination BP 116/72 mm Hg · A1c 7.6% → Within 5 years after diagnosis → in an adult with type 1 diabetes the first dilated eye exam comes within 5 years after onset, then yearly; in type 2 diabetes it comes at diagnosis. Retinopathy is asymptomatic until advanced, so waiting for symptoms misses it
  19. 34-year-old woman has a rapidly enlarging painful ulcer on her lower leg violaceous, undermined border grew from a small sore over 10 days Has inflammatory bowel disease with a recent flare T 37.3 °C · white cells 9,800/mm³ → Pyoderma gangrenosum → a rapidly enlarging, very painful ulcer with a violaceous undermined border in inflammatory bowel disease or rheumatoid arthritis is pyoderma gangrenosum: biopsy and steroids, and never debride (pathergy)
  20. 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has confirmed albuminuria ratio 140 mg/g, then 156 mg/g 3 months later Asks what most slows progression BP 138/86 mm Hg (similar at his last visit) · A1c 7.8% · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL → ACE inhibitor or ARB plus an SGLT2 inhibitor → with albuminuria and a blood pressure above the American Diabetes Association target of under 130/80 mm Hg, an ACE inhibitor or ARB plus, in type 2 diabetes with an eGFR of 20 or more, an SGLT2 inhibitor slows progression; a creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL puts his eGFR well above 20. Never combine an ACE inhibitor with an ARB
  21. 66-year-old man has a chronic non-healing ulcer on his shin arose in an old burn scar 8 months ago rolled, everted edges No better despite compression and two courses of antibiotics T 36.8 °C · pedal pulses normal → Biopsy for Marjolin ulcer → an ulcer in a chronic wound or scar with rolled, everted edges that has not healed in over 3 months needs a biopsy for Marjolin ulcer
Management Neuropathic ulcer – off-loading (total contact cast) is the single most important intervention; debride callus and necrotic tissue; glycemic control · Infection – culture only if clinically infected, deep tissue rather than a swab · Perfusion – check the ABI anyway: mixed neuroischemic ulcers are common · Charcot arthropathy – warm, swollen, red foot with no ulcer, fever or raised white count in a diabetic with peripheral neuropathy suggests it (confirm with radiographs or MRI): immobilize; rocker-bottom deformity
Why monthly A1c is wrong A1c reflects glycation across the 90 to 120 day red cell lifespan, so monthly values measure heavily overlapping windows; they add no information and prevent no complication. At goal, monthly testing is six times the 6-month schedule.
⚠︎ Two problems with the source explanation The source question for the first practice item (eye exam, pneumococcal vaccine or monthly A1c to prevent morbidity) came with two errors. 1. The pneumococcal rationale is wrong. It limited vaccination to patients over 65 or with asplenia, but every adult 50 or older is vaccinated by age, and diabetes is itself a risk-based indication in adults 19 to 49, so she is a candidate. The eye exam wins because it targets a diabetes-specific complication; vaccination addresses infection risk downstream of diabetes. 2. The attribution is off. The annual bundle and A1c intervals come from the American Diabetes Association (ADA) Standards of Care, not the USPSTF.
Buzzword → Step 2 phrasing “Microalbuminuria” → “UACR 85 mg/g” · “hyperfiltration” → “creatinine 0.7” in a diabetic · “Kimmelstiel-Wilson” → “nodular glomerulosclerosis on biopsy” · “transient albuminuria” → “he ran a 10K yesterday.”
Transferable rule

Read the outcome noun before the options: morbidity, mortality, hospitalization and benefit are four different targets, and a distractor can be the right intervention for the wrong target. The most sensitive test has the lowest detection threshold; the most specific or confirmatory test is the least likely to give a false positive. Risk factors set the prior probability and physical findings the posterior: when the exam contradicts the risk profile on three separate axes, rely on the exam.

Recurrent Respiratory Infection and Structural Lung Disease

cystic fibrosis · primary ciliary dyskinesia · antibody deficiency · foreign body · allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis when antibiotics failWhich exam finding could no immune defect produce, and when an adequate antibiotic course fails, are the eosinophils and immunoglobulin E (IgE) up?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Frequency shows that something is wrong; anatomy shows what. Antibiotic-requiring bacterial sinusitis and pneumonia crosses the gate; up to 12 self-limited viral illnesses a year is normal.

  • Heart on the right: the point of maximal impulse in the right chest is situs inversus; with recurrent sinopulmonary infection, it points to a ciliary defect: primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD). Kartagener syndrome is PCD with situs inversus, recurrent sinusitis and bronchiectasis.
  • Poor growth or greasy stools: cystic fibrosis; sweat chloride.
  • Focal and abrupt after choking: a retained foreign body; bronchoscopy.
  • Normal anatomy with absent tonsils or adolescent or adult onset: an antibody defect; quantitative immunoglobulins.
  • Antibiotics fail in a damaged airway: no improvement after a week of adequate antibiotics or unexplained lung-function decline, with eosinophilia and IgE usually above 1,000 international units (IU)/mL, is allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA), an immune response.
  • Bronchiectasis: the endpoint of any retained secretions, never the cause.
Diagnosis
Recurrent infection: the finding that picks the cause
DiagnosisThe stem showsSets it apart
PCD (autosomal recessive dynein-arm defect)Wet cough, otitis and sinusitis from infancy; distress as a term newbornHeart on the right, in 40% to 50%
Cystic fibrosis (autosomal recessive CFTR (cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator) defect)Inspissated secretions, repeated infection, bronchiectasisFailure to thrive, greasy stools, meconium ileus, nasal polyps; heart on the left
Retained foreign bodyToddler, abrupt choking episodeFocal wheeze; unilateral hyperinflation on expiratory or decubitus film
Antibody deficiencyEncapsulated sinopulmonary infection, normal airway anatomyXLA: absent tonsils and adenoids; common variable immunodeficiency (CVID): adolescent or adult onset
Heterotaxy (situs ambiguus)Congenital heart disease, midline liverAsplenia or polysplenia
When antibiotics fail in a structural lung
DiagnosisThe stem showsSets it apart
Hypersensitivity pneumonitisOrganic antigen; fever, malaise, airspace infiltratesImproves in hospital; no eosinophilia, normal IgE
StrongyloidiasisRural tropics or subtropics; eosinophilia, high IgERoaming urticaria, gastrointestinal symptoms
Granulomatosis with polyangiitisNecrotizing bronchiectasis mimicking refractory pneumoniaOlder men; sinus destruction, hemoptysis, glomerulonephritis; no eosinophilia
Nontuberculous mycobacteriaMycobacterium avium complex in cystic fibrosis bronchiectasisMonths to years; nodular, then cavitary; no eosinophilia or IgE rise
Mechanism Dynein arms – the defect makes airway cilia dysmotile and leaves embryonic nodal cilia unable to set left-right asymmetry, so laterality is randomized · Aspergillus – everyone inhales the spores and the mucociliary escalator clears them; a damaged airway (asthma or cystic fibrosis) traps them, and chronic colonization becomes Th2 hypersensitization
Management
By diagnosis PCD – daily airway clearance · ABPA – systemic glucocorticoid first-line; an antifungal such as voriconazole is added to reduce spore burden; an antifungal alone treats the antigen, not the response · Eosinophilia with tropical exposure – screen for and treat strongyloidiasis before systemic steroids, which can progress it to hyperinfection or dissemination · Heterotaxy with asplenia – encapsulated-organism prophylaxis · Cystic fibrosis – annual total IgE screens for ABPA
Practice
  1. 11-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis has a week of fever and productive cough no improvement after a week of broad-spectrum antibiotics peripheral eosinophilia IgE 3,225 IU/mL No travel, rash or gastrointestinal symptoms T 38.4°C · bilateral crackles → Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis → antibiotic failure plus eosinophilia and an IgE more than triple the usual threshold make it allergic, not bacterial. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis improves in hospital and gives no eosinophilia and a normal IgE; granulomatosis with polyangiitis affects older adults, without eosinophilia
  2. 3-year-old girl has had a chronic wet cough since infancy recurrent otitis media since infancy chest film: cardiac silhouette on the right stomach bubble on the right Growth normal for age Afebrile · oxygen saturation 98% → Primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome) → a heart on the right with chronic wet cough and otitis points to a ciliary defect: the dynein-arm defect leaves nodal cilia unable to set left-right asymmetry. Cystic fibrosis never moves the heart; heterotaxy is situs ambiguus with asplenia or polysplenia and heart disease. Confirm with nasal nitric oxide, then ciliary electron microscopy
  3. 15-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis has an exacerbation that fails initial therapy sputum grows Pseudomonas resistant to the current antibiotic eosinophil count normal IgE normal T 38.3°C · oxygen saturation 93% → Adjust antibiotics according to culture sensitivities → a resistant organism with normal eosinophils and IgE is still a bacterial exacerbation: adjust to culture sensitivities. Without the allergic markers, neither glucocorticoids nor repeat Aspergillus serology fits
  4. 2-year-old boy has his third pneumonia this year chronic loose, greasy stools weight below the 3rd percentile point of maximal impulse in the left chest No choking episode; tonsils present T 38.6°C · oxygen saturation 95% → Sweat chloride testing → with the heart on the left, poor growth and greasy stools open the cystic fibrosis axis: sweat chloride, 60 mmol/L or more. Immunoglobulins fit normal anatomy without tonsils; nasal nitric oxide fits a ciliary picture with normal growth
  5. 16-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis was diagnosed with allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis this week Aspergillus-specific IgE positive CT: mucoid impaction, finger-in-glove opacities Productive cough despite a week of antibiotics T 37.9°C · total IgE 2,600 IU/mL → Systemic glucocorticoids with an antifungal agent → the pathology is allergic inflammation: a systemic glucocorticoid first-line, with an antifungal added to reduce spore burden. Voriconazole alone treats the antigen, not the response; more antibacterial coverage treats an infection that is not there
  6. 14-month-old boy choked while eating nuts 3 weeks ago now a focal right-sided wheeze second right lower lobe pneumonia film: right-sided hyperinflation Well before the choking episode T 38.2°C · oxygen saturation 95% → Rigid bronchoscopy → abrupt onset after choking, focal wheeze and unilateral hyperinflation are a retained foreign body: rigid bronchoscopy finds and removes it. Another antibiotic course or a CT leaves the obstruction in place
  7. 14-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis comes for her routine annual review feels well baseline cough unchanged No wheeze or new sputum Afebrile · oxygen saturation 97% · lung function at her baseline → Total serum IgE → cystic fibrosis earns an annual total serum IgE, one of the few purely serologic screening intervals; CT and skin testing are not the yearly screen
  8. 5-year-old boy has had recurrent sinusitis and pneumonia since 9 months of age no palpable tonsils no cervical lymphadenopathy Heart sounds loudest in the left chest; growth normal Afebrile · oxygen saturation 97% → Quantitative serum immunoglobulins with B-cell flow cytometry → normal anatomy with absent lymphoid tissue is the antibody axis; all immunoglobulins low with B cells absent is X-linked agammaglobulinemia. Sweat chloride needs poor growth or greasy stools, and ciliary biopsy needs a ciliary picture
  9. 45-year-old man with cystic fibrosis has several months of cough and weight loss CT: nodular and cavitary opacities No hemoptysis; no recent travel eosinophils 2% · IgE 90 IU/mL · oxygen saturation 94% → Nontuberculous mycobacterial lung disease → cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis is colonized by nontuberculous mycobacteria such as Mycobacterium avium complex, rather than Mycobacterium tuberculosis: chronic over months to years, nodular then cavitary. No eosinophilia or IgE rise removes the allergic cause
  10. 8-year-old boy has a year-round wet cough unexplained respiratory distress as a term newborn chronic otitis media point of maximal impulse in the left chest Growth and stools normal Afebrile · oxygen saturation 97% → Nasal nitric oxide measurement → situs inversus appears in only 40% to 50% of PCD, so a heart on the left does not exclude it; low nasal nitric oxide supports PCD with normal situs. Intravenous immunoglobulin treats an antibody defect, and a repeat film adds nothing
  11. 34-year-old woman has asthma that is difficult to control recurrent brown mucus plugs central bronchiectasis on CT IgE 2,400 IU/mL Aspergillus skin test positive T 37.2°C · peripheral eosinophilia · oxygen saturation 95% → Systemic glucocorticoids with an antifungal agent → same disease, different structural host: asthma, like cystic fibrosis, traps the spores. A systemic glucocorticoid with an antifungal; more inhaled steroid or antibacterial therapy leaves the allergic response untreated
  12. 3-year-old girl in daycare has had 9 upper respiratory illnesses this year each self-limited without antibiotics normal examination between illnesses Older brother is well growth at the 50th percentile · Afebrile → Normal frequency of childhood viral infection → up to 12 viral illnesses a year is normal in daycare or with older siblings: reassure, no immune workup. Ciliary disease and antibody defects give antibiotic-requiring bacterial infection, not colds that clear alone
  13. 52-year-old man who farms has fever, malaise and airspace infiltrates no response to a week of antibiotics symptoms improve over 3 days in hospital No travel or rash IgE 40 IU/mL · eosinophils 1% → Identify and eliminate the inciting antigen exposure → improvement in hospital, away from the exposure, with a normal IgE and no eosinophilia is hypersensitivity pneumonitis: identify and eliminate the antigen, since removal from the exposure is what brings improvement. The allergic fungal disease needs eosinophilia and a high IgE, and the improvement already explains the picture without a biopsy
  14. 18-month-old boy has had 8 antibiotic courses for sinusitis and pneumonia older brother has the same illness mildly enlarged tonsils point of maximal impulse in the right chest Delivered vaginally without complications oxygen saturation 99% · bilateral rales and rhonchi → Primary ciliary dyskinesia → the heart on the right decides: no antibody defect displaces it. Tonsils exclude X-linked agammaglobulinemia, and 18 months excludes CVID; bilateral rales with a normal saturation argue against a foreign body; the affected brother alone separates none of them
  15. 40-year-old man from the rural tropics has refractory pulmonary infiltrates migratory urticaria abdominal pain IgE 4,100 IU/mL Infiltrates persist after 10 days of antibiotics T 37.8°C · eosinophils 18% · oxygen saturation 94% → Treat for strongyloidiasis before giving systemic glucocorticoids → eosinophilia and a high IgE with roaming urticaria, gut symptoms and tropical exposure are strongyloidiasis: treat it before any systemic glucocorticoid, which risks hyperinfection or dissemination. Antituberculous therapy explains neither the eosinophilia nor the urticaria
  16. 4-year-old boy adopted at 6 months has 6 months of nasal obstruction recurrent nosebleeds repeated antibiotics for sinusitis and pneumonia bilateral nasal polyps; digital clubbing Diffuse coarse crackles weight 3rd, height 5th percentile · oxygen saturation 93% → Cystic fibrosis → nasal polyps, clubbing and poor growth with recurrent infection point to cystic fibrosis: sweat chloride testing; newborn screening misses rarer CFTR mutations. Allergic rhinitis causes neither poor growth nor clubbing, and a vasculitis explains neither in a 4-year-old with recurrent sinopulmonary infection
  17. 15-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis has 2 weeks of productive cough no improvement after 10 days of broad-spectrum antibiotics peripheral eosinophilia total IgE 1,850 IU/mL No travel or rash Afebrile · oxygen saturation 95% → Aspergillus-specific IgE or Aspergillus skin testing → total IgE suggests; Aspergillus-specific IgE or a skin test confirms sensitization. A sputum culture or galactomannan looks for the fungus, but everyone inhales it: the disease is the immune response
  18. 17-year-old boy has had sinusitis all his life chronic productive cough infertility evaluation with his partner semen analysis: normal sperm count, absent motility No greasy stools; growth normal Afebrile · oxygen saturation 96% → Electron microscopy of respiratory cilia for dynein-arm defects → a normal count with absent motility is the ciliary pattern, and electron microscopy shows the dynein-arm defect. Cystic fibrosis often gives obstructive azoospermia or severe oligospermia from congenital absence of the vas deferens, which a normal count excludes. Klinefelter syndrome typically gives small testes with reduced testosterone, not a normal count with immotile sperm, and no sinusitis
  19. 13-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis was diagnosed with allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis sputum has grown Aspergillus repeatedly IgE 2,900 IU/mL Neutrophil count normal; no cavity on CT Afebrile · eosinophils 12% · oxygen saturation 96% → Mucus trapping defeats mucociliary clearance, allowing colonization and Th2 sensitization → everyone inhales the spores, and the mucociliary escalator clears them; trapped mucus allows colonization, then Th2 sensitization. A normal neutrophil count and no cavity remove the other two
  20. 9-year-old boy was diagnosed with primary ciliary dyskinesia at age 4 daily purulent sputum high-resolution CT: lower-lobe bronchiectasis crackles at both lung bases Takes no maintenance therapy Afebrile · oxygen saturation 96% → Begin daily airway clearance therapy → the bronchiectasis comes from failed mucociliary clearance, so start daily airway clearance; antibiotics only during exacerbations leave the secretions in place, and resection removes one lobe of a disease of the whole airway
  21. 10-year-old girl has had two pneumococcal bacteremias midline liver complex congenital heart disease no spleen on abdominal imaging Growth normal; no chronic wet cough Afebrile · HR 96/min · oxygen saturation 96% → Pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccination plus daily antibiotic prophylaxis → situs ambiguus with no spleen is the asplenia of heterotaxy: protect against encapsulated organisms with vaccination and daily prophylaxis. Intravenous immunoglobulin treats an antibody defect, and airway clearance a ciliary one
  22. 4-year-old boy has a chronic wet cough recurrent otitis media recurrent sinusitis since infancy chest film: situs inversus totalis Growth normal; tonsils present; stools normal Afebrile · HR 104/min · oxygen saturation 97% → Dynein arms of the ciliary axoneme → dynein arms power ciliary beating; their defect impairs mucociliary clearance and randomizes laterality. CFTR and Bruton tyrosine kinase defects cause infection but never move the heart
  23. 6-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis has recurrent nosebleeds greasy, foul-smelling stools weight below the 3rd percentile repeated antibiotics for sinusitis and pneumonia Bruises easily on the shins platelets 280,000/mm³ · prothrombin time prolonged → Pancreatic insufficiency with vitamin K malabsorption → pancreatic insufficiency causes malabsorption of the fat-soluble vitamins, and vitamin K deficiency causes the bleeding; neither sinus inflammation nor platelet dysfunction prolongs the prothrombin time
Common wrong answers XLA with tonsils present: it has no tonsillar or adenoidal tissue. CVID at 18 months: it presents in adolescence or adulthood. Normal childhood infection: those are viral and need no antibiotics; eight antibiotic courses are a disease pattern. Fever as proof of infection: fever, malaise and blood-streaked sputum are common in ABPA. Broader antibiotics: antibiotic failure is a finding, not a dosing problem; change the category (allergic, mycobacterial, vasculitic) before the spectrum. Tuberculosis: cystic fibrosis airways are colonized by nontuberculous mycobacteria.
Pairs with Part I Antibody Deficiencies: the airway is structurally normal, so immunoglobulin levels and the B-cell count decide. Part II Vitamins and Nutritional Deficiencies: what pancreatic insufficiency does to vitamins A, D, E and K; is the prothrombin time long? Part I Obstructive Lung Disease: the adult with brown mucus plugs.
Transferable rule

A physical finding that no immune defect could produce decides the cause of recurrent infection. When a treatment that should work fails, the failure is the finding: change the category of disease, most often infection to hypersensitivity, rather than intensifying treatment.
